item.title: Building a Virtual Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) Laboratory with Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) Method
item.dc:creator: Hyung S. Lee, Ph.D., P.E.
item.description:
GPR Article Series · GPR-01

Hyung S. Lee, Ph.D., P.E.

This article grew out of a series of Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) simulations that I originally shared through my LinkedIn posts. This is the first article in my GPR series (GPR-01), and it focuses on the basics: Using the Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) method for GPR simulations to understand how layer geometry, cracks, water, thin layers, and localized voids influence the simulated GPR response for relatively simple pavement structures. A follow-up article, GPR-02, will move beyond some of the simplifying assumptions I have in this article (i.e., homogeneous layers) and look into heterogeneous pavement models, including internal material structure, cracking, moisture, and compaction.

1. Introduction

I always thought of GPR as an attractive Nondestructive Testing (NDT) equipment because it gives us a way to investigate what is happening beneath a pavement surface without cutting, coring, or disturbing it in any other way. But that advantage also creates one of the fundamental challenges in interpreting GPR data. In the field, we do not see what is happening below the pavement surface. We only see the signal that was recorded by the GPR receiver, while the exact subsurface condition is unknown.

Again, “we only see the GPR signal, not the actual subsurface condition”. Because of this, I always wanted to approach this problem from the opposite direction. What if I create a pavement numerically, define exactly what exists below the pavement surface, transmit a virtual electromagnetic pulse through it, and examine the signal that a virtual GPR receiver records? In that environment, there is no uncertainty about the ‘ground truth’ because I know exactly what I created.

That is the basic idea behind the virtual GPR laboratory presented here. The objective is not to reproduce every detail of different commercial GPR systems out there. Instead, I wanted to use the Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) method developed by Yee (1966) to explore how different pavement geometries and subsurface conditions influence the electromagnetic response.

So, I started the experiments with an idealized pavement and then changed one thing at a time. As for me, this is what made the virtual GPR laboratory so fun – the idealized pavement serving as a reference and its GPR response being compared to those of other pavements with some simple subsurface anomalies.

To give you a little taste of what you are going to see in this article, Animation 1 shows how the transmitted GPR signal propagates through the idealized (or reference) pavement, gets reflected from a layer interface, and gets returned to the GPR receiver. Animation 2 shows the resulting GPR signal from this simulation. If you do not know what is meant by A-Scan and B-Scan, don’t worry about it for now. We will revisit those shortly.

Animation 1. GPR signal transmitted over a perfectly layered pavement.

Animation 2. A-Scans and B-Scans from GPR simulation of perfectly layered pavement.

In any event, now that we have the simulated GPR response from the idealized pavement, we can do a lot of fun things such as modifying the pavement geometry, introducing cracks, adding water, reducing/increasing layer thickness, or placing a localized void beneath the surface and watch how the measured response changes. How do you think these anomalies will affect the GPR response?

2. How This Started

Ever since the first day I used a real GPR system for assessing pavement layer thicknesses back in 2006, I always thought it would be nice to have a theoretical model that can simulate GPR response for different pavement structures. Since then, I have periodically gone back to Yee’s classic FDTD formulation for GPR to see if I could implement my own FDTD method. Only 20 years later, in 2026, I finally began experimenting with an R implementation of FDTD. The initial implementation was developed with assistance from ChatGPT and then became a computational sandbox that I could study, modify, and use for different pavement structures.

After countless failures and never-ending debugging efforts, I finally arrived at the first useful version which included a Perfectly Matched Layer (PML) boundary and an approximately 1.5-GHz GPR source. My first test was intentionally kept to a very simple pavement structure: a flexible pavement with 4.0 in. Asphalt Concrete (AC) layer and an 8.0 in. base layer over subgrade. Once I could physically recognize the transmitted and reflected signals, the model became much more interesting, not because the first successful simulation was fairly realistic, but because it gave me a baseline from which I could change one thing at a time.

The numerical implementation itself is not the focus of this article, so I will not reproduce the R code here. Instead, I will describe the model, some of the simple changes I made to the pavement structure, and what those changes did to the simulated GPR response.

Also just to make sure I say this. If you are a Python user, you might be able to do something similar to what I am doing here with gprMax. However, I have never been a Python user (at least to this date), so I do not have any experience with it. But if you do, why don’t you give something like this a try?

3. What the Virtual Experiment Is Doing

At its core, the FDTD model discretizes the spatial domain (including the different layers of the pavement as well as the layer of air above it where the GPR antenna would be located within) into a Two-Dimensional (2D) grid and advances the electromagnetic field over time. Each pavement region and the layer of air are represented by some electromagnetic properties that are typical for the respective materials, and the GPR source transmits a short pulse above the pavement surface. As the GPR pulse propagates and encounters boundaries between materials with different electromagnetic properties, part of the energy continues propagating downward while the remaining part is reflected back to the GPR receiver (or sensor).

Obviously, the GPR sensors (i.e., transmitter and receiver) are located within the layer of air above the pavement. For a given antenna position, the receiver records the reflected GPR signal amplitude as a function of time. The reflected GPR amplitude (at a given antenna location) recorded by the receiver and plotted as a function of time, is called the A-scan. As you move the GPR antenna, it will repeat this process and you will end up with a series of A-scans along the distance traveled by the antenna. Stacking these A-scans side-by-side (and frequently shown as a 2D color-coded image where the x-axis is the distance traveled by the GPR antenna, y-axis is time as was in the A-scan, and the color represents the returned amplitude) gives us the B-scan representation that you may be familiar with. That is what I showed in Animation 2 earlier for the idealized or reference pavement.

The numerical model used for these experiments is a 2D FDTD model with Convolutional Perfectly Matched Layer (CPML) boundaries on all four sides. The antenna is represented as a finite-width transmitter and receiver rather than a point source. It is intended to approximate the behavior of a 1.5-GHz ground-coupled GPR antenna, not to reproduce the proprietary internal design or exact emitted waveform of a commercial GPR antenna. For those of you that may wonder, Table 1 summarizes some of the important parameters I used throughout the simulations.

Table 1. Parameters used in the 2D FDTD GPR simulation.

Category Parameter Value / Configuration
Numerical grid Grid spacing dx = dz = 0.005 m (5 mm)
Numerical grid Grid size 300 x 280 cells (approximately 1.50 m x 1.40 m)
Antenna approximation Nominal center frequency 1.5 GHz
Antenna approximation Effective Tx/Rx position Transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) at 30 mm above pavement
Antenna approximation Tx-Rx horizontal offset 0.060 m (6 cm)
Material properties Air Dielectric constant = 1.0; Electrical conductivity = 0 S/m
Water Dielectric constant = 80.0; Electrical conductivity = 0.03 S/m
Asphalt concrete Dielectric constant = 5.0; Electrical conductivity = 0.001 S/m
Granular base Dielectric constant = 7.0; Electrical conductivity = 0.003 S/m
Subgrade Dielectric constant = 12.0; Electrical conductivity = 0.010 S/m
B-scan acquisition Scan interval 0.020 m (2 cm)

4. Experiment #1 —The Reference or the Boring Pavement Structure

The best place to begin is the “least realistic”, or the idealized pavement I already showed you in Animations 1 and 2. Again, this pavement has a 4.0 in. AC and an 8.0 in. base over subgrade. Because it is an idealized pavement, the layer interfaces are perfectly flat and the material properties (i.e., dielectric constant and electrical conductivity) are known without any uncertainty or variability. For this pavement, the GPR wavefront reaches the layer boundary in a “smooth” manner and the reflected energy returns in a relatively organized manner.

The simple and unrealistic geometry of this pavement may not be all that meaningful and you may think that the simulation results look “boring” at best. But it does show how the GPR signal propagates and reflects under an idealized scenario where there are no anomalies whatsoever. We can watch the transmitted pulse leave the antenna, interact with the pavement surface, continue through the AC, encounter the AC/base interface, and then interact with the deeper base/subgrade interface. The corresponding A-scan provides the receiver’s view of those events.

In summary, the results from this simulation (Animations 1 and 2) showed us two important things: (1) how the electromagnetic field is physically propagating and reflecting inside the modeled pavement and (2) what the GPR receiver ultimately sees and records. That baseline is valuable because we want to understand how this may change once we start introducing some anomalies into the pavement structure.

5. Experiment #2 — Real Pavements Are Not Perfectly Flat

The baseline pavement is useful, but it is also boring. Real pavement layers do not have a perfectly uniform thickness along a roadway. To see how this could affect the GPR response, I decided to introduce a little variability into both the AC and base thicknesses.

So for Experiment #2, I varied the AC and base thicknesses using a normal probability distribution. The AC thickness was varied with a mean of 4.0 in. and a standard deviation of 0.4 in. while the base thickness was varied with a mean of 8 in. and a standard deviation of 0.75 in. See animations 3 and 4 for the results.

Animation 3. Propagation of GPR signal through the reference pavement and a pavement with nonuniform thickness (Animation_3_LinkedIn_Post).

Animation 4. A-Scans and B-Scans from the reference pavement and a pavement with nonuniform thickness (Animation_4_LinkedIn_Post).

The difference is immediately visible, right? In the uniform pavement, the AC/base and base/subgrade interfaces were comparatively easy to identify. Once the interfaces became nonuniform, those reflections became less clean.

Why? The GPR wave no longer encounters a perfectly flat interface. Instead of reflecting the energy back to the receiver in one orderly pattern, the irregular interface redirects the energy in many different directions. Consequently, the irregular interface caused increased scattering of the GPR signal, potentially reducing the reflected energy received by the antenna.

This is an important reminder when interpreting real GPR data. A weak or messy interface does not necessarily mean the interface is absent. The geometry of the interface itself can change how much reflected energy makes it back to the antenna.

Also, just in case you wonder why the pavement layers are colored differently in Animations 2 and 4. Animation 2 was created as I was preparing this article, not when I was working on my LinkedIn posts. So, Animation 2 has a more “recent” color scheme that I prefer to use. But for the contents coming from my LinkedIn posts, I will use the same color scheme I used there.

6. Experiment #3 — What Do Closely Spaced Bottom-Up Cracks Do?

In Experiment #3, I wanted to introduce an intentionally exaggerated “fatigue” crack pattern. The purpose was not to claim that this geometry represents a real cracked pavement. It was a controlled numerical experiment that I designed to make the interaction between the wave and the crack tips easy to observe.

I started with the reference pavement and inserted the bottom-up cracks throughout the AC layer. Each of the modeled bottom-up cracks were 1.0 cm wide, began at the bottom of the AC layer, terminated at mid-depth, and were spaced every 2.0 cm. See the animation below for how the GPR signal propagates through this pavement.

Animation 5. Propagation of GPR signal through the reference pavement and a pavement with idealized bottom-up cracks (Animation_5_LinkedIn_Post).

Compared with the intact pavement, the cracked model produced additional scattering and a noticeably distorted receiver response. The interesting behavior occurred at the crack tips. Because there are so many crack tips at the same depth and were closely spaced, their individual responses began to overlap. Collectively, they almost looked like an additional or ‘artificial’ interface even though no continuous material boundary existed at that depth.

Figure 1 shows the A-scans and the B-scans from both pavements (Sorry, I did not necessarily create animations for all B-scans, but I hope the figure tells the story just as well). The same concept helps explain why a localized feature and a distributed feature can look very different in a B-scan. A single crack tip may generate a localized hyperbolic-type response (if the crack tip was wide enough for the GPR signal), while many closely spaced responses can overlap and begin to look more like a continuous reflector.

7. Experiment #4 — Put Water at the AC/Base Interface

As you may already know, the dielectric constant of water is much higher than any other materials. Thus, water almost always affects the GPR signal propagation and reflection dramatically because it creates a strong electromagnetic contrast. To visually see that effect, I started with the reference pavement again and modeled a thin layer of water (5.0 mm or approximately 1/5-in.) trapped at the AC/base interface over a horizontal distance from approximately 0.5 m to 1.0 m.

This is not intended to be a realistic representation of how moisture exists in a real pavement by any means. A real “wet pavement” would likely involve changes in moisture content within the unbound layers, and therefore electromagnetic properties. I will get into a little bit of that in the next GPR article but here, the thin water layer was used simply to make the effect easier to see. The results are shown below in Animation 6 and Figure 2.

Animation 6. Propagation of GPR signal through the reference pavement and a pavement with a thin layer of water at the AC/base interface (Animation_6_LinkedIn_Post).

The first thing I want to point out is the strong reflection from water. In the simulated A-scan and B-scan, the response associated with the bottom of the AC appeared at roughly 4.5 ns in both pavements, but the amplitude of the GPR signal reflected from water was nearly comparable to the direct coupling between transmitter and receiver.

The second thing is that because so much energy was reflected from the water-bearing interface, the GPR signal kept “bouncing” between the pavement surface and the water layer. This bouncing of GPR signal resulted in additional peaks that appeared at approximately 6.0 ns and 7.5 ns in the A-scan and B-scan. Those later peaks are NOT additional pavement interfaces. They were repeated reflections or “ringing” of the GPR signal traveling back and forth between the water and the pavement surface (i.e., the GPR energy is “trapped” between the water and the pavement surface).

And because most of the GPR energy is trapped above the water, there is not enough GPR energy left to propagate down to the base/subgrade interface. This is why it is very difficult (or close to impossible) to see the base/subgrade interface in the A-scan and B-scan results. This is exactly the kind of situation where simply counting peaks in an A-scan could lead to a misleading interpretation.

8. Experiment #5 — What If the Asphalt Layer Is Too Thin?

For Experiment #5, I wanted to ask a more practical question. What happens when the layer we want to identify is thin enough such that GPR reflections from its top and bottom interfaces occur very close together in time?

This one was fairly easy for me. Starting with the reference pavement which had 4.0 in. of AC, I simply changed the thickness to 1.5 in. Animation 7 and Figure 3 show the results from this experiment.

Animation 7. Propagation of GPR signal through the reference pavement and a pavement with a thin AC (Animation_7_LinkedIn_Post).

For the reference pavement with 4.0 in. of AC, the GPR signal reflected from the bottom of AC is clearly visible at approximately 4.5 ns. However, for the pavement with 1.5 in. AC, the corresponding GPR signal occurred at approximately 3.5 ns and began to overlap with the much stronger signal from the pavement surface.

The important thing is not simply about a thin layer producing a shorter travel time for the GPR signal. It is resolution or the interaction between the GPR antenna frequency and the thickness of the layer. If there is a layer that is fairly thin for the given antenna frequency, the two interfaces – at the top and at the bottom of this thin layer – can produce responses that are blended together. This is why the GPR signal from the bottom of the thin AC layer may look like it is part of the surface reflection rather than a separate layer boundary.

I personally thought that this experiment also provided a need for further signal-processing approaches for decomposing the blended GPR signal when there is a thin layer. I have not tried it myself, but for anyone interested, Chen et al. (2026) provides a methodology that you could use for decomposing the blended GPR signal due to thin layers.

9. Experiment #6 — Why Does a Void Make a Hyperbola?

One of the most well-known features of a GPR B-scan is the hyperbola – or often casually called parabola – which is the “signature” of GPR associated with many localized subsurface objects. Pipes, reinforcing bars, and voids are classic examples.

If you ask Google, it may tell you that the signature hyperbola is because the GPR sends the signal in a “cone-shaped” manner and picks up the reflected signal before and after the antenna passes over the anomaly. Well… for Experiment #6, I wanted to see that visually.

So, again starting with the reference pavement, I inserted a circular void with a diameter of 6.0 in. at a center depth of approximately 10 in. below the pavement surface.

See Animation 8 for how the GPR signal propagates and reflects back to the antenna. Note that I did something different here. Rather than including the reference pavement again, I included the 4 different locations for the GPR antenna relative to the void, so that I can show what happens as the antenna approached, passed over, and moved away from the void.

Figure 4 shows the resulting hyperbola in the corresponding B-scan (Note: due to the different scales used for the x and y axes in this graph, the void looks more or less like an oval rather than a circle).

Animation 8. Propagation of GPR signal through a pavement with a void (Animation_8_LinkedIn_Post).

Do you agree with Google that the “GPR sends the signal in a cone-shaped manner”? In my opinion, this is probably a very simplified version of what it truly is. But you know what? In the Falling Weight Deflectometer (FWD) world, we love to talk about the “Influence zone” to explain why the deflections further away from the loading plate is representative of the subgrade response. Do you see the similarity here?

In any event, what we see here is that the GPR antenna does not need to be directly above the void before the energy can interact with it. As the antenna moves, the propagation path to the localized target changes. The arrival time therefore changes from one A-scan to another, depending on the location of the antenna. Of course, if the antenna is closer to the target, that means less time for the GPR signal to travel back to the antenna. Stack those A-scans side-by-side and you get the signature hyperbola in your B-scan.

10. What Did These Simple Experiments Tell Me?

I emphasize again that the experiments from this virtual GPR laboratory are NOT intended to reproduce an actual field GPR survey. I hope the value comes from doing the opposite – simplifying the problem enough that the cause of a particular response can be isolated for us to understand. So, here is a quick summary of what we saw in this article.

  • A perfectly flat layer interface produces very clean, recognizable GPR results. However, the geometry of the interface itself may affect the scattering of the GPR signal and change how much energy is reflected back to the antenna.
  • Closely spaced discontinuities can produce overlapping responses that may look like an artificial layer in the GPR scans.
  • A strong dielectric contrast such as water can dominate the response, create repeated reflections (i.e., ringing), and may not show you the layer interfaces below the water.
  • Thin layers may be a little more challenging to identify because the GPR signals reflected from the top and bottom interfaces of the thin layer may start to overlap.
  • Hyperbolic responses in GPR B-scans arise from changes in travel time as the antenna moves relative to a localized target.

11. Where This Goes Next — GPR-02

There is also an obvious limitation to all experiments I showed here. The pavement layers are still treated largely as homogeneous materials. Real asphalt concrete is not a uniform block. It contains aggregate, asphalt mastic, and air voids. Unbound base and subgrade layers are heterogeneous as well. Once that internal structure is represented explicitly, the electromagnetic field has many more boundaries and contrasts to interact with.

That is where my next GPR article (GPR-02) will begin. Instead of asking how GPR responds to idealized layers and isolated anomalies, the next article will move toward a heterogeneous virtual pavement and examine how material structure, cracking, moisture, and compaction influence the simulated response.

The basic question remains the same. If we know exactly what is inside the pavement, what will the GPR data actually look like?

So, GPR-01 is intentionally the fundamentals article. GPR-02 will pick up from here by replacing the largely homogeneous layers used above with heterogeneous pavement materials and asking a harder question: can we still identify and interpret the response when the pavement itself is generating substantial internal reflections and scattering?

Here is a little preview of the pavement cross-section that we will see in GPR-02. Stay tuned!

Animation 9. Heterogeneous pavement model showing crack propagation and water intrusion (Animation_9_LinkedIn_Post).

12. References

item.title: Four Traffic Speed Deflectometer (TSD) Myths: Confirmed, Busted, or Plausible?
item.dc:creator: Hyung S. Lee, Ph.D., P.E.
item.description:
TSD Article Series · TSD-01

This article is based on the presentation I gave at the 2026 FWD User Group (FWDUG). The FWDUG presentation can be downloaded from my ResearchGate site: FWDUG_Presentation.

One distinction I need to make before we jump into the article. In this article, a Traffic Speed Deflection Device (TSDD) is defined as any equipment designed and built to measure pavement deflection at high speeds, regardless of the technology used. Traffic Speed Deflectometer (TSD), on the other hand, is one type of TSDD that specifically uses doppler lasers for measuring pavement surface velocity (or deflection velocity). So, TSDDs include TSD, Rolling Wheel Deflectometer (RWD), Raptor, etc. That extra “D” matters!

1. Introduction

Over the past decade or so, I have spent considerable time working with Traffic Speed Deflectometer (TSD) theory and data, developing computational tools for simulating pavement response under moving loads, and asking questions about assumptions that are commonly made when interpreting TSD data.

These are also some of the questions I received most frequently from my colleagues. While some of them understood what I was verbally telling them, some others struggled to follow my verbal explanation without any visual proof in front of them. So, I decided to call these questions (that I receive the most regarding TSDs) the 4 myths and wanted to explain them with some of the theoretical proofs that I generated over the past year or so.

Several of these questions have appeared in bits and pieces throughout my LinkedIn posts, and I will provide the links to those posts where applicable. Here are the 4 myths and I will provide you my current conclusions on whether they are Confirmed, Busted, or Plausible in the remainder of this article. These questions may initially seem independent, but they are not. The answer to one myth also helps set up the next.

TSD Myths
Myth #1 Pavement deflection under moving load (e.g., TSDD) has good correlation with deflection under impact load (e.g., FWD).
Myth #2 TSD deflection slopes can be integrated to provide deflections.
Myth #3 You MUST consider all TSDD axles (or tires) in your model.
Myth #4 TSD deflection slopes can be used for backcalculating layer moduli, including subgrade modulus.

Note that there is a PowerPoint file that I used to present this material at the 35th Falling Weight Deflectometer User Group (FWDUG) meeting that was held in September, 2026. This article will closely follow the material that I had in that presentation. The original presentation, including the complete slide deck and animations, is available on my ResearchGate website.

📊 View / Download Original Presentation on ResearchGate ↗

2. Scope and Definitions

The analyses presented here are limited to continuous pavement systems, specifically flexible pavements. Joints and other pavement discontinuities are not considered. My conclusions will be 100% based on theoretical simulations, i.e., no field data was used in the analyses presented in this article.

For TSDs equipped with doppler lasers, the deflection slope is defined as deflection velocity (measured by the doppler lasers) divided by vehicle speed:

where S is deflection slope, Vdef is the measured deflection velocity and Vv is vehicle speed.

It is emphasized that the relationship in Equation 1 only holds for “Continuous Pavements”. For pavements with joints or any other discontinuities, this relationship doesn’t necessarily hold true and I will try to develop another article on this subject in the future. But for this article, we are only interested in continuous pavements that Equation 1 can be used for calculating the deflection slope.

One Distinction That Must Be Made Clear

Is the deflection slope a “measured” parameter from TSD? I would say YES. This is because there is no uncertainty in calculating the deflection slope from the deflection and vehicle velocities. In other words, if you and I start with the same deflection and vehicle velocities, we both will arrive at the same deflection slope.

What about deflection itself from the TSD? Is this a measured parameter? This is clearly NO. Going from deflection slope to deflection requires some sort of integration. However, depending on the assumptions you make, you may end up with completely different deflections from the same deflection slope. For this reason, deflection from TSD is an analyzed parameter, NOT a measured parameter. A little more discussion on this topic is provided under Myth #2 and I might even develop another article on this specific topic.

3. Myth #1 — Pavement deflection under moving load (e.g., TSDD) has good correlation with those under impact load (e.g., FWD)

At first glance, this may sound reasonable. Both the Falling Weight Deflectometer (FWD) and Traffic Speed Deflection Devices (TSDDs) apply a known load to a pavement surface and measure the resulting deflection. If both devices are evaluating pavement structural condition, it is tempting to expect the measured deflections to correlate well.

Mechanically, however, TSDDs (i.e., moving loads) and FWDs (i.e., impact loads) are totally different. According to a paper that my friend, Doug Steele (1968-2023) and I co-authored, some of the differences in loading characteristics include the following (Steele et al., 2021).

  • Loading mode: impact versus moving load

  • Loading rate: speed effects

  • Load configuration: single plate versus dual tires

  • Half-axle versus full-axle configurations

  • Constant target loads versus dynamic variations

For the above-referenced study, Doug had asked me to make a lot of ViscoWave runs for both the FWD and the Rolling Wheel Deflectometer (RWD) – A TSDD that we were developing at the time. The pavement structures we simulated at the time, are shown in Table 1.

Table 1. Pavement layer properties studied in the previous study by Steele et al. (2021).

Layer Thickness (in) Modulus (ksi) Temperature (˚F)
Asphalt Concrete 4, 8, 12, and 16 Sigmoidal Fcn 50, 70, and 90
Base 8, 10, and 12 40, 60, and 80 N.A.
Subgrade 120 10, 20, and 30 N.A.

To provide some sample results we got from the above study, Figure 1 and Figure 2 show the pavement deflections differ under different loading modes and different loading configurations, respectively. Yes, the deflections are different, but they are not that different. So, were there any correlations between the FWD and RWD deflections?

Figure 1. Effect of loading mode on pavement deflection (Steele et al., 2021).

Figure 2. Effect of loading configuration on pavement deflection (Steele et al., 2021).

Figure 3 shows the correlation between the maximum deflections obtained under the FWD (9-kip peak load) and the RWD (18-kip single axle with dual tires, i.e., total of 4 tires traveling at 60 mph). Well… Not bad, right? The figure clearly shows a decent correlation with an impressive R2 value of 0.85! But is this the end of the story? It is not. Let’s revisit this in this myth.

Figure 3. Comparison of maximum FWD and RWD deflections (Steele et al., 2021).

3.1 Revisiting the comparison

Looking back at Table 1, you may think Doug and I had covered a pretty broad range of pavement structures. The Asphalt Concrete (AC) thickness ranged from 4.0 to 16.0 in. and the base thickness ranged from 8.0 to 12.0 in. What about subgrade? Table 1 shows that the subgrade thickness was fixed at 120.0 in. This means that there was a stiff bedrock at 132.0 to 148.0 in. below the pavement surface depending on the AC and base thicknesses. Is this subgrade thickness of 120.0 in. adequate for all pavements we see in the field? My experience says NO, and this is what we are about to revisit.

For the myths to be presented in this article, I generated 1,770 pavement structures for simulation. Table 2 shows the thickness and modulus of the pavement layers. Note that I intentionally fixed the AC and base thicknesses so that I can highlight the influence of subgrade.

Table 2. Pavement layer properties used for the TSD myths in this article.

Layer Thickness (in.) Modulus (ksi)
Asphalt Concrete 8 (fixed) 100–500
Base 10 (fixed) 10–100
Subgrade 100–300 2–18

For Myth #1, the FWD responses (i.e., deflection time histories) were obtained from ViscoWave (https://github.com/leehyu20/ViscoWave) by simulating an impact load of 9-kip peak load with a duration of 25-ms applied on a 12-in diameter loading plate. The moving-load responses were obtained from DSteele by simulating an 18-kip single axle with dual tires (i.e., 4 tires total with 4.5-kip load on each tire).

Here is an animation I generated to show the TSDD deflections and the FWD time histories for all 1,770 pavements.

Animation 1. TSDD Deflection vs. FWD Time History (Animation 1 LinkedIn Post).

From the above results, I extracted the deflections at several different offsets (0, 8, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48, 60, and 72 in.) from the center of the FWD load plate as well as from the center of two dual tires of TSDD. Here is the animation that shows how these deflections at different offsets compare. Watch carefully when the subgrade thickness and/or modulus changes.

Animation 2. 1:1 Comparison of FWD and TSDD deflections (Animation_2_LinkedIn_Post).

Did you see what happened? Here is a summary of what I saw. When AC or base modulus changes for a given subgrade condition (i.e., thickness and modulus), the FWD-vs-TSDD relationship generally moves in a relatively consistent direction as indicated in Figure 4. For example, all the points move around the red curve for a given subgrade condition but the points will move around the green curve for a different subgrade condition.

Figure 4. All 1,770 FWD-vs-TSDD deflection comparisons. What happens when AC and/or base modulus changes for a given subgrade condition.

What does that mean? It means that you might be able to establish a decent correlation for a given subgrade condition. However, when the exact same pavement (i.e., same thickness & modulus for both AC & base) is sitting on a different subgrade, you will get a completely different correlation. In other words, when subgrade modulus or thickness changes, the entire FWD-vs-TSDD deflection relationship will shift left or right as indicated in Figure 5.

So, how would you develop a correlation between FWD and TSDD deflections for a variety of pavements? Remember, the AC and base thicknesses were never varied in this simulation. So, imagine what is going to happen once you start varying AC, base, and subgrade thicknesses altogether. The correlation will likely look much worse than what you see in Figure 4 or 5.

3.2 Why does the subgrade change the entire relationship or correlation?

The keyword here is “INTERACTION”. Under moving dual-tire/full-axle/full-truck configurations, stress and response fields from multiple tires start interacting (or overlapping if you prefer this terminology) within the pavement system.

Consider the dual tires of a half-axle shown in Figure 6. Each tire would have its own influence zone (note that this influence zone is over-simplified here as it is only intended to illustrate the concept). But because the duals are quite close to one another, the influence zones from the 2 tires start overlapping within the AC layer. The consequence is shown in Figure 7 where the deflection is plotted along the transverse direction. See the “w” shape deflection below the tires? That shape is due to the interaction.

Figure 6. Interaction of dual tires due to influence zone overlapping.

Figure 7. Simulated response under dual tires showing interaction (w-shaped deflection).

But that is not the end of the story. The 2 tires shown in Figures 6 and 7 only correspond to one half of the full axle (i.e., half-axle). There are 2 more tires on the other side! Figure 8 shows the full-axle with 4 tires and the influence zones (again, the influence zones are over-simplified here) from all tires. See where the interactions occur? Again, the dual tires on each side of the axle start interacting within the AC. But more importantly for this figure, the 2 half-axles start interacting within the subgrade layer.

Figure 8. Interaction of dual tires due to influence zone overlapping.

So, what happens due to this interaction between the 2 half-axles? As shown in Figure 9, the overall response or deflection under this full-axle, when plotted along the transverse direction, shows a much larger “W” shape. Fortunately or unfortunately, given the typical configuration of modern truck/trailer systems and the typical pavement thicknesses we have nowadays, this interaction between the 2 half-axles is almost always going to occur in the subgrade layer.

So, what’s the catch here? The TSDDs are generally instrumented on one side of the vehicle (i.e., on one of the half-axles). However, it doesn’t mean it is only measuring the response under that instrumented half-axle. The instrumentation feels the entire axle due to the interaction. This significance or the degree of this interaction is largely dependent on the subgrade because that’s where the interaction occur!

On the flip side, FWD is always applied on a single plate. So, there is no interaction from multiple loads whatsoever. So, the discrepancies that you see in Figures 6 and 7 between the FWD and TSDD deflections are primarily caused by the subgrade where the interaction between the 2 half-axles take place.

MYTH #1 VERDICT — BUSTED!

MYTH #1 IS BUSTED!

Myth #1 is busted if the assumption is that TSDD and FWD deflections can be directly correlated through one general relationship. The simulations clearly show that the relationship is strongly influenced by the underlying pavement system, particularly the subgrade where the interaction between the 2 half-axles occurs. In order to generate a relationship between FWD and TSDD deflections across different pavements, we may need additional insights from physics or other mechanistic methods to properly address the difference between a single load (FWD) and multiple loads (TSDD). Remember, it is all about the SUBGRADE.

4. Myth #2 — TSD deflection slopes can be integrated to provide deflections

This statement almost sounds trivial mathematically. The deflection slope is nothing but the derivative of the deflection, D(x), with respect to x. Therefore, calculus says we can simply differentiate the deflection curve to obtain the slope curve we want. Mathematically, this relationship is written as the following.

Yes, it is true. As illustrated in Figure 10, if you start with a known deflection curve, you will end up with a unique slope curve. But does it work the other way around?

Well, all we had to do to obtain the slope curve from a deflection curve was to differentiate the deflection curve. So, all we have to do to obtain the deflection curve from a slope curve is to integrate the slope curve. Right…? The answer is no, No, NO, and Hell NO!

Recall from your calculus class... When you integrate a function mathematically, it always comes with an “Integration Constant”. So, the correct mathematical notation for integrating the slope curve to obtain the deflection curve, is given as the following.

where C is the unknown integration constant. What does this mean? It means we can end up with an infinite number of deflections unless we know what the C value is specifically. 4.1 The reference-sensor assumptions

Well… If we do not know the integration constant C we need for integration, how are we integrating the slope to get the deflections from TSD?

One thing we also need to discuss before the integration process is that all TSDs have one or more “Reference Doppler Sensor(s)”. The Reference Sensor measurement is subtracted from all other doppler measurements, and it is not reported to the end user. I do not want to dive too deep into this, but let’s just say this is needed to correct for the vehicle motion (i.e., so that we can see the pavement response rather than the vehicle response). Most of the recent TSDs have this reference sensor located at approximately 121.0 in. from the instrumented axle (i.e., xref = 121 in).

There are 2 primary assumptions behind how the slopes are being integrated today. These assumptions are mathematically expressed as the following.

and

Yes, that’s just me trying to look fancy with those equations. All in all, it only means that both the deflection (Equation 4) and the deflection slope (Equation 5) are assumed to be ZERO at the reference sensor location.

So, how is the integration carried out and what is the effect of the above assumptions? For those of you that want to learn more, I made a separate graphic on this topic which you can download from my ResearchGate site: TSD_Integration. We will keep the discussion here relatively brief and focus on the consequences of the above assumptions.

The Zero-Deflection assumption in Equation 4 basically shifts the entire deflection curve up or down such that the deflection at the reference sensor location crosses the x-axis. This is illustrated in Figure 12. I am going to call this the “Shifting Error”.

The absolute deflections (e.g., D0, D8, … , D72) you get from integrated TSD deflections are always affected by this “Shifting Error”!

One thing to note about the shifting error is that it does not affect some of the frequently used Deflection Basin Parameters (DBPs). As an example, the Surface Curvature Index (SCI) which is defined as D0 – D12, is clearly not affected by this shifting error because both the D0 and D12 get shifted by the same amount, and the shifting error naturally cancels out in the calculation.

Figure 12. Zero-deflection assumption shifts the entire deflection up or down.

The Zero-Slope assumption in Equation 5 rotates the entire deflection curve about the reference sensor location, forcing the non-zero slope at the reference sensor location to become zero. This is illustrated in Figure 13 and I will call this the “Rotation Error”.

Unlike the shifting error, this rotation error affects everything including the DBPs. Going back to the DBP example we had up there, the D0 and D12 needed for calculating the SCI are not shifted by the same amount when this rotation happens.

The “Rotation Error” affects EVERYTHING including absolute deflections (e.g., D0, D8, … , D72) and relative deflections or Deflection Basin Parameters (DBPs)!

Figure 13. Zero-slope assumption rotates the deflection about the reference sensor location.

4.2 Can the integration be improved?

Do you believe in the Zero-Deflection assumption in Equation 4 and/or the Zero-Slope assumption in Equation 5?... I do NOT! Well… then is there a different way we could integrate the deflection slopes? Possibly!

Again, because I do not believe that both the deflection and deflection slope should be zero at the reference sensor location, I decided to try something slightly different. First, I wanted to recover (if possible) the non-zero slope at the reference sensor location and second, I wanted to assume that the deflection was zero further away from the TSD axle.

These thoughts led me to what I would call a “Two-step Cubic Hermite Spline Fitting” procedure. Sounds fancy but it only means that I am doing the cubic spline fitting twice. This process is graphically illustrated in Figure 14.

  1. The first spline is fitted through the measured slopes plus another location further away from the reference sensor (say 400 in.) where the slope is assumed to be zero. The only purpose of this first spline is to estimate the nonzero slope at the reference sensor.

  2. The non-zero slope at the reference sensor location estimated from the first spline is added to all of the measured slopes (because this value was subtracted during measurement).

  3. A second spline is then fitted through the corrected slopes and the estimated slope at the reference sensor. The location where the slope was assumed to be zero during the first spline fitting (again, say 400 in. to be consistent with what I had in Step 1) is also included. This second spline is used for numerically integrating the deflection slope.

Figure 14. Two-step cubic Hermite spline concept used to estimate the reference sensor slope before integration.

So essentially, I used a different location for the zero-deflection and zero-slope assumption. The above text shows I used 400 in. for this new location, but I actually used several different locations at 172, 300, 400, and 500 in. were tested. The 172 in. location may sound like a weird location, but it is the location that is halfway between the driving axle and the TSD axle for ARRB’s most recent TSD configuration. In any rate, all these “new reference locations” resulted in similar results, so I will only provide those from 400 in. as the new reference location.

MYTH #2 VERDICT — ABSOLUTELY BUSTED!

MYTH #2 IS BUSTED!

Myth #2 is absolutely busted if you are relying on purely mathematical integration of TSD deflection slope. This is mainly because there is no way for us to recover the information that has already been lost: the non-zero slope and non-zero deflection at the reference sensor location. Trying different reference locations may help a little, but it is still a wild “guess”.

If you still want to integrate the TSD deflection slope to obtain the deflection… maybe you will need some additional guidance from “Physics” or “Mechanics”.

Also remember that the current integration scheme for TSD deflection slope will always give you 2 different errors.

  1. Shifting Error resulting from the Zero-Deflection assumption. This will not affect some of the DBPs (e.g., SCI) that describe the “shape” of the deflection basin.

  2. Rotation Error resulting from the Zero-Slope assumption. THIS AFFECTS EVERYTHING.

Remember that the subgrade modulus is one of the most important parameters in conventional flexible pavement design. The subgrade modulus is typically estimated from the deflection that is measured at certain distances (typically between 36 in. and 60 in.) from the load. The integrated deflection you get from TSD is affected by both shifting and rotation errors.

5. Myth #3 — You MUST consider all TSDD axles (or tires) in your model

The above myths dealt with 2 fundamental questions: (1) how TSDD response differs from FWD response and (2) whether the TSD deflection slopes can be integrated to provide absolute deflections. The third myth turns to a more practical modeling question.

When we simulate a TSDD, do we really need to model the entire truck and trailer?

At this point, I would like to emphasize that this myth is limited to forward simulation only. Backcalculation is a different problem, and we will deal with that separately in Myth #4.

The motivation for asking the above question is primarily due to computational efficiency. A full TSDD model (i.e., truck and trailer) will contain multiple axles and many individual tire loads. If our primary interest is the pavement response near the instrumented TSD axle, it is tempting to ask whether we can simply model that axle and ignore the rest of the vehicle. A reduced model can be considerably more efficient, particularly when thousands of forward simulations are required for sensitivity studies, optimization, backcalculation development, or even AI/ML training.

But Myth #1 already gave us a reason to be cautious. We saw that pavement response is not controlled only by what happens directly beneath an individual tire (or half-axle). Stress and deformation fields spread through the pavement structure, and their interaction can become especially important in the deeper layers. In fact, the interaction between the two half-axles was one of the reasons the relationship between FWD and TSDD deflection became strongly dependent on the subgrade. In Myth #3, I am asking essentially the same question at a larger spatial scale. How much do the other axles of the TSDD influence the response measured near the TSDD axle?

5.1 Can We Simulate Only the TSD Axle?

Figure 16 shows an example comparison of the deflections obtained from a single tire and the full TSD models. You can clearly see the deflections due to the additional axles (i.e., steering and driving axles) within the full TSD model that are not present in the single axle model. The more important observation, however, is what happens near the TSD axle itself. The two deflection curves are not identical, but they seem really close to one another. Right?

Figure 16. Deflections from single axle and full TSD models with minimal interaction between TSD axles.

The results shown in Figure 16 may seem encouraging for the single-axle approximation at first glance. If the response around the measurement axle is nearly the same, why can’t we ignore all the other axles and save some time in running those simulations? Well… the particular example shown in Figure 16 shows minimal interaction between different axles of the TSD. The real problem is that the amount of interaction is not always minimal like the one shown in Figure 16. As the pavement structure changes and the amount of interaction becomes more significant between different axles, the influence of the driving axle(s) on the response near the TSD axle also changes.

For most pavements, the interaction between different axles becomes much more noticeable than what is shown in Figure 16. See Figure 17 as an example which shows some significant interaction between the TSD axles. You can clearly see that the deflection from the single axle model may not be as good as what it was in Figure 16. Once again, it is the pavement structure, particularly the deeper supporting layers, that controls how broadly the response from one axle spreads before it begins interacting with the response from another axle.

Figure 17. Deflections from single axle and full TSD models with significant interaction between TSD axles.

So, Myth #3 is not asking whether the additional axles produce their own deflection basins because they obviously do. The question is whether the additional axles of the TSDD affect the response at the location we have the TSDD measurement system, and, if they do, whether the resulting error is large enough to matter for the intended application.

MYTH #3 VERDICT — CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE

This myth is CONFIRMED if the objective is to avoid the simplification error or if you are not willing to tolerate any error.

MYTH #3 IS CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE!

Do we really need to model all axles and tires of the TSDD? The answer depends on what you are trying to accomplish?

If you are not willing to tolerate any modeling error associated with axle simplification, then the myth is CONFIRMED. In this case, you need to simulate the full TSD or, at a minimum, the TSD axle and the driving axle(s) that may influence the measured response.

But engineering models are almost always a compromise between fidelity and efficiency. If an error of the magnitude observed here is acceptable for the intended application, then a single-axle model can be a useful approximation. In that case, the myth becomes PLAUSIBLE rather than universally confirmed.

So, I would encourage you to ask yourself what you are trying to do with your forward models. Depending on what your goal is… instead of simply asking yourself “Can I simplify the TSDD to one axle?”, the better question might be:

How much modeling error am I willing to tolerate for the computational efficiency I gain?

Before I finish my thoughts on this myth, I also need to make one thing very clear. The errors I showed you in this myth should not be taken as universal error bounds for every TSDD. ARRB, Greenwood, Falkor, ICC-IMS, and other systems such as Raptor use different axle spacings, axle loads, tire configurations, and vehicle geometries. The interaction between axles, and therefore the error associated with reducing the vehicle to a single axle, should be evaluated separately for the specific device and application.

6. Myth #4 — TSD deflection slopes can be used for backcalculating layer moduli, including subgrade modulus

Finally, the first three myths have led us toward this myth.

Myth #1 showed that the subgrade plays a major role in the relationship between impact loading and moving load response. In addition, Myth #1 showed that TSDD deflections are not well correlated to FWD deflections.

Remember that the subgrade modulus is one of the most important parameters for pavement design. However, Myth #2 showed that we cannot get the absolute deflections (which we need for estimating the subgrade modulus) by integrating the TSD slopes mathematically.

Myth #3 then showed that simplifying the full TSD vehicle to a single axle during modeling introduces errors in both deflection and slope.

So perhaps we should take a different route, rather than keep trying to get the “absolute deflections” from TSD by integrating the slopes or trying to correlate the TSD deflections to those from FWD.

What if we just use the deflection slope itself?

More specifically, the question we want to ask is if the TSD slopes contain enough structural information for us to backcalculate the pavement layer moduli—including the subgrade modulus? And, based on what we learned in Myth #3, what happens to the backcalculated results if we simplify the forward model to a single TSD axle?

As I discussed in Myth #2, the measurement from the reference doppler laser is subtracted from those of all other dopplers to remove the vehicle motion from the measurements. This is an important extension of Myth #3. A forward simulation error of several percent may appear relatively modest when we are simply comparing deflection or slope. But backcalculation is an inverse problem. Small differences in the modeled response can propagate into much larger differences in the material properties required to reproduce the response. In other words, the simplification error in the forward simulation does not necessarily remain in the range when we go to backcalculation.

The result therefore reinforces the importance of matching the forward model to the actual TSDD configuration when the objective is structural backcalculation. A reduced single axle model may still be useful, but the computational savings come with a much larger uncertainty in the backcalculated layer moduli.

6.6 An Important Clarification: This does Not mean ±5% backcalculation error when we use field data

The full-truck result needs one very important clarification. The ±5% error observed here should not be interpreted as evidence that TSD backcalculation with field data will produce backcalculated pavement moduli within ±5%.

The results I showed you here are controlled synthetic, matched-model backcalculations. The pavement response was generated using the same general theoretical framework used in the backcalculation analysis, the layer thicknesses were known without errors, and the true moduli were known exactly. Under these conditions, the study primarily tests whether the offset-slope response contains sufficient information for backcalculating the input properties.

Field measurements introduce additional sources of uncertainty that are not represented in this synthetic experiment such as measurement noise, load and speed variation, pavement temperature, uncertainty in layer thickness, viscoelasticity of AC, nonlinear or stress-dependent unbound materials, and other device- and site-specific effects.

So the conclusion from this myth is not to say that TSD backcalculation with field data can be performed with about ±5% error. The conclusion is narrower and, I think, more importantly at this stage (under a controlled mechanistic framework), TSD offset slope contains sufficient information to recover the AC, base, and subgrade moduli. Field validation is the next step.

MYTH #4 VERDICT — CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE

For full truck matched-model synthetic backcalculation, Myth #4 is CONFIRMED. The TSD offset slopes contained sufficient structural information to backcalculate the AC, base, and subgrade moduli, with errors mostly within approximately ±5% for the 1,770 pavement structures evaluated here.

For single axle backcalculation, the myth is PLAUSIBLE at best. The recovered moduli showed substantially greater error, mostly within ±20%. Whether that level of error is acceptable depends on the intended application and your engineering judgement.

MYTH #4 IS CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE!

TSD slope does not have to be treated merely as an intermediate quantity that must be converted into absolute deflections for further analysis. The offset slope can be treated directly as the measurement domain for backcalculation. The full truck slope-based backcalculation successfully recovered all three pavement layer moduli including the subgrade within ±5% error.

The TSD measures deflection slopes (or velocities to be more exact), NOT deflections. Why not use what was measured by the equipment?

7. The Four-Myth Scorecard

Taken together, I hope the 4 myths tell you a connected story about how TSD measurements should be interpreted and modeled.

Myth #1 showed that TSDD and FWD responses are not simply interchangeable. Myth #2 showed that although TSD measures deflection slope, absolute deflections cannot be obtained through purely mathematical integration without additional, mechanistic- or physics-based guidance. Myth #3 then moved to forward simulation and showed that simplifying the TSDD vehicle to a single axle can provide substantial computational efficiency, but at the cost of increased error. Finally, Myth #4 showed why that distinction becomes even more important in backcalculation – a relatively modest error in forward simulation can translate into a considerably larger error in the backcalculated layer properties.

Collectively, these results point to a common lesson: TSD slope is a structurally informative measurement in its own right, but extracting reliable pavement properties from it may require a more mechanistic framework that properly represents the pavement system, the measurement reference, and the loading configuration.

8. Engineering Implications

These myths suggest that TSD analysis should be approached as a moving load mechanics problem, rather than a “high-speed analogue of FWD”. That distinction has practical consequences for both interpretation of TSD measurements and development of forward and inverse analysis methods.

  • FWD and TSDD measurements may correlate under defined conditions, but that relationship should not be assumed to remain transferable across pavement structures, particularly when subgrade conditions change.

  • TSD deflection slope may contain useful structural information in its own right. Converting slope measurements to absolute deflection, however, requires additional information or constraints beyond pure mathematical integration.

  • Reduced axle representations can provide substantial computational efficiency, but the resulting approximation error should be quantified for the specific TSDD configuration, pavement conditions, and intended application.

  • For backcalculation, offset deflection slopes should be treated as the equivalent of measured responses.

The broader implication is that TSD slope does not necessarily need to be converted into an FWD-like deflection basin before it becomes useful for pavement evaluation. A mechanistic model that directly predicts the quantities measured by the TSD provides an alternative path: compare measured and predicted slopes in their native form and use those responses directly for structural inference.

9. Limitations and Next Steps

The analyses presented in this article are primarily theoretical and computational. They were intentionally designed to isolate individual mechanics and modeling assumptions so that their effects could be examined independently. Consequently, the results should not yet be interpreted as validation of a complete field-ready TSD backcalculation framework.

The most important next step is field validation. In particular, the slope-based backcalculation approach should be evaluated using measured TSD data from pavement sections for which layer thicknesses and material properties have been characterized. Such comparisons would provide a much stronger conclusion on whether the structural information demonstrated in the synthetic analyses can be extended to field conditions.

Several additional effects should also be investigated, including viscoelasticity of AC layer, nonlinear or stress-dependent behavior of unbound materials, temperature, dynamic axle loading, measurement noise, and device-specific sensor locations and geometry. These factors were intentionally excluded from the analyses presented here.

The conclusions regarding reduced axle configurations should likewise be regarded as configuration-specific rather than universal. The magnitude and spatial distribution of approximation error depend on axle spacing, axle loads, sensor offsets, pavement structure, and the particular TSDD platform. Comparable sensitivity analyses should therefore be performed before adopting a reduced loading representation for another device or application.

10. Closing Thoughts

The four myths explored in this article began as separate technical problems, several of which first appeared in my individual LinkedIn posts. I hope putting these together reveals a more coherent story about how TSD measurements should be interpreted and modeled.

Perhaps the simplest way to summarize the four myths is this: TSDD is not an FWD traveling at highway speed. Although both devices are used to characterize pavement structural response, the loading mechanisms, measurement quantities, and underlying mechanics are fundamentally different. Those differences should be recognized rather than treated as complications to be removed.

That, to me, is the most useful outcome of this exercise. The purpose is not simply to label the myths as Confirmed, Busted, or Plausible for the sake of a Mythbusters-style scorecard. It is to understand why an assumption works, where it begins to break down, and what the underlying pavement mechanics are telling us.

The four myths therefore point toward a broader principle for TSD analysis: work as closely as possible with the physics of the measurement itself. Instead of forcing TSD measurements into the framework of an FWD test, the analysis should recognize the moving load system, the vehicle configuration, the measurement reference, and the response quantities that the TSDD actually measures. Or, stated more simply:

Don’t interpret TSD by asking how closely it can imitate FWD. Interpret TSD based on the mechanics of what TSD actually measures.

Purpose and Scope

DS-01 introduced DSteele from the perspective of its development, motivation, implementation, and application to moving-load and Traffic Speed Deflectometer (TSD) analysis. This companion article documents the mathematical formulation underlying the model. The derivation that follows is retained from my original, unpublished DSteele formulation manuscript with only the surrounding context reorganized for this article.

The purpose of DS-02 is not to reproduce the DSteele source code. Rather, it is to document the mechanics and mathematical structure of the solution: the governing equations, transformation to the wavenumber domain, spectral-element stiffness formulation for finite layers and the semi-infinite halfspace, treatment of elastic and viscoelastic properties, global assembly, moving surface loading, and inverse-transformation of the response back to the physical domain.

Mathematical Development of DSteele

As indicated in one of my previous LinkedIn posts (original LinkedIn post), I derived the mathematical derivation of DSteele by hand. The hand-written derivation extended across more than twenty pages and included the displacement-potential solution, evaluation of displacement and stress components at layer boundaries that were ultimately used to construct the spectral-element stiffness matrix.

Development of the formulation was iterative. Because an error discovered late in the derivation could propagate into the layer stiffness matrices, portions of the derivation were restarted and checked repeatedly before being translated into code. The photographs below preserve part of that original development record. They are included as technical provenance for the formulation, not as a substitute for the mathematical development that follows.

Figure 1. Original handwritten derivation developed during the formulation of DSteele. The derivation progressed from the governing equations and displacement potentials through finite-layer displacement and stress relationships used to construct the spectral-element stiffness matrices.

Figure 2. Close-up from the original handwritten development of the finite-layer displacement relationships, including evaluation of displacement components at the upper and lower layer boundaries prior to their organization in matrix form.

Detailed DSteele Formulation

The formulation proceeds from the three-dimensional equations of motion for an elastic, homogeneous continuum. Helmholtz decomposition is then used to express the displacement field in terms of scalar and vector potentials. For a load moving at constant speed, the solution is written in a two-dimensional Fourier representation so that derivatives with respect to space and time can be handled algebraically in the transformed domain.

The resulting harmonic solutions are used to derive stiffness matrices for two-noded finite-thickness layers and a one-noded semi-infinite element. Elastic or viscoelastic layer properties are incorporated into those element relationships, after which the individual elements are assembled into the global pavement system. The transformed nodal response is solved for each wavenumber pair and subsequently transformed back to obtain the pavement response associated with the moving load. Details of DSteele formulation is provided in the following.

The preceding derivation provides the mathematical foundation implemented in DSteele. At the element level, each finite pavement layer is represented by a stiffness matrix in the frequency domain, while the bottom layer can be represented directly as an element of finite thickness or a semi-infinite element. These element relationships are assembled into the global pavement system in a manner analogous to finite-element assembly.

Although the formulation is developed in terms of the full three-dimensional displacement and stress fields, DSteele was developed with moving-deflection applications as a central motivation. item.title: DSteele: A 3D Spectral-Element Model for Pavement Response under Moving Loads
item.dc:creator: Hyung S. Lee, Ph.D., P.E.
item.description:
DSteele is a mechanics-based moving-load pavement response model developed with Traffic Speed Deflectometer (TSD) applications as a central motivation. This article introduces its origin, implementation, early evaluation, and the research questions it has enabled.

Overview

DSteele is a dynamic, three-dimensional (3D) spectral-element or finite-layer model developed to simulate flexible pavement responses under moving vehicle loads, with Traffic Speed Deflection Device (TSDD) applications as a central motivation.

The model calculates pavement response under a moving load by solving the 3D equation of motion semi-analytically in the frequency domain for each pavement layer of finite thickness. In this sense, each layer acts as a spectral element. Multiple layers (or elements) are then connected in a manner similar to the finite element method to construct the global stiffness matrix, which is solved for pavement responses including deflection. More importantly for TSD analysis, DSteele can provide deflection slope directly as a model response without approximating it numerically from a series of independently calculated deflections.

The formulation supports both elastic and viscoelastic material representations for asphalt materials. The viscoelastic material input takes the form of a time-domain relaxation modulus represented by a four-parameter sigmoidal function.

The initial DSteele implementation was developed in 2023. Its computational engine is written in C++, while an Excel-based interface is used to define pavement structures, moving loads, vehicle speed, and response output locations.

This article introduces why DSteele was developed, its implementation and early evaluation, and the research questions it subsequently enabled, many of which were discussed across my LinkedIn posts. This article is intended only as an overview. A future, separate article will document the mathematical formulation in greater depth.

1. Why I Developed DSteele

Traffic Speed Deflection Devices (TSDDs), which include TSDs with Doppler lasers as well as devices such as the Rolling Wheel Deflectometer (RWD) and Raptor that use distance lasers, represent a fundamentally different methodology for measuring pavement surface deflection compared with stationary impact devices such as the Falling/Heavy Weight Deflectometer (F/HWD). Rather than stopping at discrete locations and applying an impact load, a TSDD measures pavement deflection while traveling at highway speed.

For those of you who know me, you may have heard of ViscoWave. It is a dynamic, finite-layer model for analyzing F/HWD (i.e., impact-load) time-history data that I developed as part of my Ph.D. work. After I finished my Ph.D., I personally continued developing ViscoWave for moving-load or TSDD applications, but I never really had a research project that needed it.

My first exposure to a real TSDD research project came when my friend and colleague, Doug Steele (1968-2023), was leading a research effort to develop the RWD. After I finished my Ph.D. work, Doug pulled me into his RWD research team, and I had my first real occasion to use ViscoWave to simulate moving loads. Although the RWD research was completed using ViscoWave’s moving-load implementation, it had one critical drawback. While it was fairly efficient for analyzing F/HWD time-history data, it was computationally inefficient—and therefore time-consuming—for simulating or analyzing moving loads.

If you knew Doug, you could probably imagine him telling me that we needed something that could simulate moving loads faster and more efficiently. Yes, that is exactly what he did almost every day when he saw me in the office. I had ideas that could potentially lead to a new solution, but since our RWD research was discontinued and I became busy with other things, it never became reality.

In January 2023, we lost Doug in a tragic accident. At his funeral, I thought about what Doug had been telling me for so long: I needed to develop a new solution for moving loads. After spending countless late nights and weekends working on it, my first public description of the new solution appeared in a LinkedIn post in June 2023. I named the solution DSteele in honor and loving memory of my friend, Doug Steele.

2. What DSteele Solves

DSteele represents a layered pavement system in three dimensions. Each finite pavement layer (or element) is described by its material properties (i.e., modulus, density, Poisson’s ratio, and damping) and thickness. It solves the stress-wave propagation problem for a layered pavement system under vehicle loads traveling at a constant speed. At a conceptual level, the analysis process is as follows.

  1. Define the layered pavement structure and material properties.
  2. Define the moving wheel-load configuration and vehicle speed.
  3. Transform the variables from the physical domain, , to the frequency (or wavenumber) domain, , in the horizontal plane.
  4. Construct the frequency-domain stiffness matrix based on the semi-analytical solution for each layer that makes up the pavement.
  5. Assemble the layer stiffness matrices into a global stiffness matrix and solve for the nodal responses in the frequency domain.
  6. Inverse-transform displacement and other pavement responses back to the physical (spatial) domain.

3. DSteele Implementation

As mentioned, the computational engine of DSteele was implemented in C++, while a developmental MS Excel interface serves as the primary user interface. This separation allows the computationally intensive spectral-element calculations to be conducted efficiently, while the spreadsheet provides a convenient way for the user to communicate inputs and outputs with the C++ engine and visualize the results without repeatedly importing or exporting files through separate software.

4. Why Deflection Slope Matters for TSD

In this context, Traffic Speed Deflection Devices (TSDDs) include devices designed and built to measure pavement deflection from a moving platform, whereas the Traffic Speed Deflectometer (TSD) refers to a specific type of TSDD that uses Doppler laser sensors to measure pavement response.

It is important to emphasize that the Doppler lasers do not measure distance or displacement directly. Instead, they measure vertical pavement deflection velocity. For continuous pavements (e.g., flexible pavements), the deflection velocity can be divided by the vehicle velocity to yield the deflection slope, which is essentially the derivative of deflection in the longitudinal direction.

Deflection velocity, or equivalently deflection slope under the steady moving-load relationship, is a particularly unique response associated with TSDs. Other TSDDs that use distance lasers do not rely on deflection slope (or velocity) at all. To support analysis of different TSDDs that exist today as well as those that may be developed in the future, DSteele was therefore developed to calculate not only deflection but also deflection slope directly within the solution. As will be discussed in the mathematical formulation article, this quantity can be obtained naturally in the frequency domain.

5. Early Evaluation against 3D-Move

During early development, DSteele response was compared with 3D-Move for a common pavement/loading case. The purpose of this comparison was to check whether the independently developed moving-load solution produced a physically consistent deflection history with comparable response magnitude and shape.

The curves show close agreement in overall response shape and peak deflection, with a small systematic difference visible over much of the time history. This comparison is therefore best described as an early model-to-model evaluation rather than comprehensive validation. Broader verification and validation would require a documented suite of analytical, numerical, and/or measured benchmarks.

6. From DSteele to DSteele V2

As the range and complexity of DSteele analyses grew, computational runtime became increasingly important. Development of DSteele V2 focused on accelerating the frequency-domain calculations without changing the fundamental physical formulation.

The idea behind V2 development was to interpolate the high-frequency portion of the frequency-response function and to take advantage of symmetry in the 2D Fourier transform. In the cases I tested during development, these changes reduced runtime by more than a factor of 20 compared with the original implementation.

This improvement was purely numerical and related to the implementation of DSteele; it did not change the underlying formulation or derivation. The details may therefore be documented in a separate article in the future.

7. What DSteele Has Enabled

DSteele has allowed me to explore several topics in greater depth as I studied the TSD. A short list of these topics is provided below.

  • Sensitivity of modeled deflection and deflection slope.
  • Investigation of assumptions used when integrating TSD slope to construct deflection.
  • Separation of shifting and rotation errors in reconstructed deflection basins.
  • Backcalculation using deflection slopes directly at Doppler-sensor locations.
  • Evaluation of full-truck versus reduced axle/load representations.
  • Comparison and correlation of TSD and FWD responses under different loading conditions.
  • Dimensional analysis of moving-load pavement response.
  • Development of a machine-learning surrogate for rapid prediction of DSteele response.

Some of the topics above have already been covered in bits and pieces across my LinkedIn posts. I plan to develop several of them into longer articles so that the work has a more permanent home.

8. DSteele in Motion

A moving-load model is easier to understand when the response is visualized in an animation. For this reason, I also developed a number of 2D and 3D visualizations of DSteele results, along with other related simulations. I plan to develop separate articles around some of the visualizations that originally appeared in my LinkedIn posts.

For this introductory article, the visualization below shows pavement deflection under a moving standard single axle, originally posted on LinkedIn.

Continue the DSteele series

The next article will focus on the detailed mathematical formulation of DSteele, including the governing equations, transformed-domain solution, spectral-element stiffness formulation, semi-infinite halfspace, viscoelastic representation, and global assembly.
